analysis.one_liner: Grants farmland to Black farmers, expands farm credit, and forces large meatpackers to buy more on the open market.
analysis.headline: Despite 36 House sponsors and no recorded opposition, the bill never received a hearing or vote — it was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would address a long history of USDA discrimination against Black farmers. It would buy farmland and give it free to eligible Black individuals (up to 160 acres each, at least 20,000 grants a year), expand zero-interest farm loans, fund Black land-grant colleges, create a paid Farm Conservation Corps for young adults, and give a Black farmer-run civil rights board power to review USDA discrimination complaints. It would also rewrite livestock market rules: large meatpackers would have to buy at least half their cattle and hogs on the open spot market instead of through their own captive supply, and could no longer own or feed the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.who_benefits: Black farmers and ranchers seeking land and credit; socially disadvantaged farmers and ranchers eligible for priority in USDA programs and easier loan access; young adults from socially disadvantaged groups who would join a paid Farm Conservation Corps with housing and medical care; historically Black colleges and universities receiving $500 million a year for agriculture programs; and independent livestock producers and contract poultry growers who would gain stronger legal rights against large packers and integrators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Black farmers and socially disadvantaged ranchers

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs USDA to buy agricultural land at no more than fair market value and convey it free to eligible Black individuals — up to 160 acres each, with at least 20,000 grants per year funded at $8 billion a year.

It expands credit: land-grant recipients and socially disadvantaged farmers would get direct operating loans at zero percent interest for the first seven years with 24 months of payment deferral, and a new federally chartered National Socially Disadvantaged Farmer and Rancher Bank would lend $1 billion at 30-year Treasury rates to community lenders serving these farmers.

Black farmers who filed claims in the Pigford v. Glickman discrimination settlements and still owe USDA loans would have that debt forgiven, plus a grant worth 30 percent of the forgiven amount and reimbursement of seized funds.

USDA civil rights enforcement would be overhauled: an independent oversight board would review appealed discrimination complaints with fact-finding power, an Equity Commission would study the agency's treatment of Black farmers, a foreclosure moratorium would apply while a civil rights complaint is pending, and USDA could no longer have its General Counsel involved in investigating complaints against itself.

A Farm Conservation Corps would enroll up to 20,000 young adults ages 18–29 per year from socially disadvantaged groups, paying them farmworker wages and providing housing, food, clothing, and medical care while they apprentice on small farms.
Historically Black colleges and universities would receive $500 million a year to start and expand agriculture-related courses of study, plus a $20 million-a-year USDA/1890 National Scholars Program.

Large meatpackers would have to buy at least 50 percent of their daily slaughter volume through open spot-market sales from independent producers, would be banned from owning or feeding livestock they slaughter, and poultry companies could no longer penalize growers based on factors outside the growers' control in the poultry 'tournament' pay system.

Poultry growers, livestock producers, and swine contractors would gain rights to data used to set their pay, protection from retaliatory termination, and attorney's fees if they win a suit under the Packers and Stockyards Act.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund roughly $11 billion or more each year for a decade — $8 billion for land purchases, $1 billion for farmer-support nonprofits, $1 billion for the Farm Conservation Corps, $1 billion for the new farm bank, and $500 million for HBCUs, among other programs. Large meatpackers and poultry integrators would bear the cost of restructuring how they buy livestock, some portion of which could show up in wholesale meat prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates large sums directly from the Treasury — $8 billion a year for land grants, $1 billion a year for qualified entities, $1 billion a year for the Farm Conservation Corps, $1 billion for the farm bank, and $500 million a year for HBCUs — a multi-hundred-billion-dollar ten-year commitment with no offset.

Conveyed land would carry an easement restricting it to agricultural use in perpetuity, and USDA would hold a right of first refusal when the recipient later wants to sell, limiting the recipient's ability to borrow against or profit from the land's full value.

The requirement that large packers buy half their daily volume on the spot market and the ban on packer ownership of livestock would force major changes in how the largest meat companies procure cattle and hogs; packers and some economists argue such mandates reduce the supply-chain flexibility and quality control that integration provides, and added procurement costs could eventually reach consumers.
The bill's benefits are targeted by race and social disadvantage, raising fairness and legal questions for other farmers who face the same narrow margins but do not qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill makes a very large, sustained public investment to reverse documented USDA discrimination that shrank Black landownership, and its livestock-market provisions would strengthen independent producers against a handful of dominant meatpackers. The fiscal cost is real and the land-grant design trades wealth-building for permanent farmland protection — a defensible but debatable choice. The packer provisions are the most contested: they would genuinely restructure a concentrated market, but their effect on retail meat prices is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Alma Adams of North Carolina introduced the Justice for Black Farmers Act of 2023 on February 24, 2023.

The bill was referred the same day to five committees — Agriculture, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, the Judiciary, and Budget — each with jurisdiction only over the provisions that fall under it, so no single committee controlled the whole bill.
Thirty-five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; all 36 sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.
The action history records no activity after the day of referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, in either chamber, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill's land grants, credit expansion, civil rights oversight, and livestock-market reforms therefore never advanced past introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators kept their existing purchasing arrangements with no new spot-market requirements or ownership restrictions. USDA's operations and its handling of civil rights complaints continued unchanged, and Black farmers and ranchers received no new land, credit, or recourse.

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams
for.role: Lead sponsor, U.S. House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Justice for Black Farmers Act of 2023 and recruited 35 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership (Chair Glenn Thompson)
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the referral was the last recorded action on the bill.

against.name: House Financial Services, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Budget Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions under their jurisdiction after the bill was referred to them on introduction day.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 House supporters were Democrats — the sponsor plus 35 of 216 House Democrats as cosponsors, with no Republican support recorded — and no vote was ever taken, so opposition never had to declare itself.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (beef, pork, and integrated livestock processors)
industries.note: The bill would require covered packers to buy at least half their daily slaughter volume through open spot-market bids and would bar them from owning or feeding the livestock they slaughter, unwinding decades of captive-supply arrangements that let a few firms control prices paid to ranchers. Independent producers and consumers in concentrated markets would gain bargaining power; the packers' model of control would shrink.

Live poultry dealers would be brought directly under Packers and Stockyards enforcement, the poultry 'tournament' pay system could no longer grade growers on inputs the company controls, and growers would gain rights to the data behind their pay and protection from retaliation — directly limiting the integrators' power over contract growers.

industries.industry: Nonprofits and 1890 land-grant institutions serving Black farmers
industries.note: The bill would route land identification, training, succession planning, and legal advocacy through 'qualified entities' funded at $1 billion a year, and give $500 million a year to historically Black colleges, making these institutions the standing channel for delivering land access — a lasting institutional role as well as new revenue.

The USDA would buy farmland at no more than fair market value from willing sellers at a scale of $8 billion a year, giving owners a ready buyer; a government buyer at that scale could also bid up land prices for farmers who are not sellers.

industries.industry: Community lenders and credit unions serving socially disadvantaged farmers
industries.note: A newly chartered federal bank would lend to eligible credit unions and community development financial institutions at 30-year Treasury rates, and the CFPB would gain enforcement authority over Farm Credit System discrimination claims, expanding capital and oversight for these lenders' customers.
